title: False friends and first expressions
topic: common false friends and everyday expressions
why: Before the big review of the basics, this lighter lesson defuses the false friends that trip up English speakers (embarazada, constipado, éxito, largo…) and gives you the expressions that make a conversation sound natural in Spain: vale, venga, ¡qué pena!, no pasa nada.

{"lessons": ["

False friends that trip up English speakers

Spanish and English share thousands of words from Latin, so you can often guess what a word means. That's a gift, but also a trap: some words look familiar and mean something completely different. Here are the most common ones, and the most embarrassing.

SpanishMeansWatch out
embarazadapregnantembarrassed → avergonzada
constipado / constipadahaving a cold, congestedconstipated → estreñido
exquisito / exquisitadelicious (a dish)used mostly for food
la salidathe exitfrom salir (to go out), not a “sale”
el éxitosuccessexit → la salida
largo / largalongnot “large”! wide → ancho
contestarto answerto contest, dispute → discutir, protestar
la carpetathe folder, the bindercarpet, rug → la alfombra
el vasothe glass (for drinking)vase → el jarrón
la ropaclothesnot “rope”! a dress → el vestido
molestarto bother, to disturbnothing to do with “molest”
quitarto take off, to removeto quit → dejar, salir de

The most famous one: an English speaker who wants to say “I'm embarrassed” and says estoy embarazado announces… that he's pregnant. For embarrassment, say me da vergüenza (I'm embarrassed), and learn it as a set phrase.

", "

Examples so you never get them wrong again

The best way to lock in a false friend is to see it in an everyday sentence.

Mi hermana está embarazada: ¡voy a ser tío!My sister is pregnant: I'm going to be an uncle!
No voy a trabajar hoy: estoy muy constipado.I'm not going to work today: I have a really bad cold.
La tortilla de tu madre está exquisita.Your mother's tortilla is delicious.
Perdone, ¿dónde está la salida?Excuse me, where's the exit?
Su restaurante tiene mucho éxito.His restaurant is very successful.
Esta calle es muy larga, pero no es muy ancha.This street is very long, but it isn't very wide.
Te escribo, pero nunca contestas.I write to you, but you never answer.
¿Me das un vaso de agua? Los papeles están en la carpeta verde.Can you give me a glass of water? The papers are in the green folder.
¿Te molesta la música? — No, no me molesta.Does the music bother you? — No, it doesn't bother me.
Me quito la chaqueta porque hace calor.I'm taking off my jacket because it's hot.

Notice that molestar works like gustar: the thing that bothers you is the subject (me molesta el ruido, me molestan los coches).

Learn false friends in pairs: largo / ancho, la salida / el éxito, el vaso / el jarrón. Linking the trap with the right word helps you stop mixing them up. Two more classics for later: actual means “current”, not “actual”, and la librería is a bookstore, not a library.

", "

Everyday expressions

These little words come up in every conversation in Spain. Knowing them will make you sound much more natural.

ExpressionMeaningExample
valeOK, all right¿Quedamos a las ocho? — Vale.
vengacome on!; OK then; right, bye¡Venga, vamos! / Venga, hasta luego.
¡qué guay!so cool! awesome! (informal)¿Vas a Ibiza? ¡Qué guay!
¡qué pena!what a shame!¿No puedes venir? ¡Qué pena!
no pasa nadano worries, it's fine— Lo siento. — No pasa nada.
¡ojo!watch out! careful!¡Ojo, el suelo está mojado!
¿qué tal?how are you? how's it going?¡Hola! ¿Qué tal?
de nadayou're welcome— Gracias. — De nada.
¡qué rico!so tasty! yum!¡Qué rica está la paella!

A few details

  • Vale is typically Spanish: you'll hear it ten times a minute. In Latin America, people tend to say está bien or ok.
  • ¡Qué guay! is informal and specific to Spain. In Mexico, people say ¡qué padre!, in Argentina ¡qué bueno!
  • ¡Qué pena! means “what a pity”, nothing to do with pain or a penalty: it's light.
  • Rico means “rich”, but for food it means “tasty”; it agrees with the noun: ¡Qué ricas están las croquetas!

The pattern ¡qué + adjective! works with lots of words: ¡Qué bonito! (how beautiful!), ¡Qué raro! (how weird!), ¡Qué bien! (great!). Don't forget the opening ¡ and the accent on qué.
